# Diagnosing Heated Wing Mirrors on a 2004 VW Passat B5.5

When you swap the control switch and only one side of your heated wing mirrors responds, it is tempting to assume the switch is the sole culprit. However, in electrical systems like those found in a 2004 VW Passat B5.5, a single-point failure often masks multiple underlying issues. The fact that the right mirror warms up while the left remains cold indicates a specific circuit path is broken, likely at the component level rather than the control unit.

The heating element in the wing mirror acts as a simple resistive load. When you flip the switch to the "heated" position, voltage travels from the battery through the fuse box, into the switch mechanism, and then splits to power both the left and right mirrors simultaneously. If the switch is indeed faulty, it might fail to complete the circuit for one leg of that split while still completing the other. This would explain why one mirror works and the other does not, even if you have swapped the switch or if the previous issue mentioned in your diagnostics was related to the switch logic.

However, the most common failure point in these vehicles is the heating element itself. These elements are embedded within the plastic housing of the mirror glass. Over time, thermal cycling causes micro-cracks to form in the resistive wire or breaks the connection where the wire exits the glass. This usually happens at the edge of the mirror assembly where the glass meets the metal bracket. If you inspect the left mirror closely while it is cold, you might notice that the plastic housing feels significantly colder than the right side, confirming that no current is flowing through the internal trace.

To determine if the heating element is broken before tearing apart the assembly, you can perform a simple continuity test with a multimeter. Remove the mirror glass from the bracket by unscrewing the retaining bolts at the base of the housing. Locate the two electrical contacts on the back of the mirror glass; these are typically small metal tabs or pins connected to the heating wire and the ground.

Set your multimeter to the continuity or resistance (Ohms) setting. Place one probe on the positive contact tab and the other on the negative contact tab.
- If you see a reading in the range of 10 to 50 Ohms, the heating element is intact. The lack of heat was likely caused by the switch failing to send power to that specific leg.
- If your multimeter reads "OL" (Open Loop) or infinite resistance, the heating element has an open circuit and is broken.

If the continuity test confirms an open circuit, replacing the mirror glass is the required fix. This is not an easy repair in the sense of a software toggle or a simple fuse replacement; it involves mechanical disassembly. You must carefully pry the mirror glass out of the plastic housing to avoid snapping the delicate tabs holding the heating element wires. Once removed, you can replace the glass with a new one that comes pre-wired and ready to install.

There is a trade-off here regarding cost versus effort. Some owners attempt to solder new heating elements onto the old glass, but this is often unreliable because the existing wire exit points are fragile and prone to breaking again under thermal stress. It is generally safer to replace the entire mirror glass assembly.

Regarding your other issue involving the switch: if the heating element on the left side is confirmed broken via multimeter, replacing the switch will not fix the cold mirror problem. You can then address the switch separately if it is also faulty, effectively killing two birds with one stone only if both components are defective. But based on the symptoms of one working and one failing, a localized hardware failure in the left mirror glass is the primary suspect.
